Q: etcd for HA Patroni/Postgres - etcd user/password authentication A:

I figured out from the patroni docs that you can make etcd username/pw known to Patroni by using the environment variables

Q: How can i develop a fullstack android app within 6 hours? A:

In a 6-hour hackathon, the most important thing is not building a complex app, but delivering a small, fully working system. Your app should focus only on core features like authentication (login/register), a main dashboard with a RecyclerView, and basic add/view/delete functionality using SQLite. Avoid unnecessary components like fragments, view pagers, or complex navigation. Instead, keep navigation simple using activities only, and focus on making a smooth flow rather than adding many features.

The working flow of your app should be simple and linear. For example, the user opens the app → logs in or registers → reaches the main screen → sees a list of items → can add or delete items → and returns to the updated list. This ensures your app has a clear and predictable structure. All data should flow from user input → SQLite database → RecyclerView → UI display. Keeping this flow simple will help you avoid confusion and reduce development time.

For implementation, use SQLiteOpenHelper for database handling, and create only the essential tables like users and items. Keep your database structure simple and avoid over-normalization. For UI, use ViewBinding, RecyclerView, CardView, and basic widgets like TextInput and Buttons. Keep logic minimal and avoid overengineering—writing code directly in activities is acceptable in hackathons if it saves time.

To make your app future-proof (without wasting time), follow a few basic practices. Use constants for database names and columns, separate database logic into one helper class, and avoid hardcoding values everywhere. Maintain a simple project structure like: db/, ui/, and models/. This keeps your code organized enough to debug but still fast to develop.

Speed is the key in hackathons, so divide work efficiently among team members. One member should handle database logic, another should focus on UI and design, and the third should handle integration and testing. Work in parallel instead of waiting for one person to finish. Also, use templates, copy-paste similar patterns, and rely on Android Studio’s built-in tools to save time.

Your development strategy should be strictly time-based. Spend the first 30–45 minutes on planning and schema design, 1–2 hours on database and authentication, 2–3 hours on the core feature (RecyclerView + CRUD operations), and the remaining time on testing and UI polish. Avoid trying to make everything perfect—focus on completing features first, then improving them.

Finally, remember that hackathons are about delivering a working prototype, not a perfect product. Many teams fail because they try to build too much or follow complex architecture. Instead, follow the principle of “build small, keep it working, and finish everything”. If your app is complete, stable, and demonstrates the idea clearly, you will stand out more than teams with unfinished complex apps.

Q: Problem with error NumPy's new string extension dtype A:

There can be two problems:

  1. if column code1 was created only with numbers then it may have dtype as int and it may not allow to put strings. It may need to convert it to object to accept strings, numbers, etc.
df["code1"] = df["code1"].astype(object)
  1. np.where() may expect that both results will have the same type of dataand it may try to convert one of them to type of other. It may need to return numbers for both result - e.g. -1 instead of "SAME" - and later replace all -1 with string "SAME"
df["code1"] = df["code1"].astype(object)  # allow for strings, integers, etc. 

for i in range(1, len(df)):
    df["code1"].values[i - 1] = np.where(
         (df["TICKER"].values[i - 1] == df["TICKER"].values[i])
          & (df["BD"].values[i] == df["SD"].values[i - 1]),
         -1,  # <-- number instead of string
         1000,
    )

df.loc[df["code1"] == -1, "code1"] = "SAME"  # convert all -1 to "SAME"

I would do it without np.where and for-loop but using .shift(-1) to have values from both rows (i-1 and i) in one row

It still need to set df["code1"].astype(object) to allow strings, integers,et c.


df["code1"] = df["code1"].astype(object)

# set default value for all rows except last
df.loc[df.index[:-1], "code1"] = 1000

# select all rows which need `"SAME"`
mask = (df["TICKER"].shift(-1) == df["TICKER"]) & (df["BD"] == df["SD"].shift(-1))

# set `"SAME"` for selected rows
df.loc[mask, "code1"] = "SAME"

Q: How can changes in .tpp template implementation files trigger recompilation in a Makefile? A:

Add the .tpp file as a dependency of the object file:

# MRE.tpp is included by MRE.hpp, so it must be a dependency
# but must NOT be compiled directly.
TestMRE.o: TestMRE.cpp MRE.hpp MRE.tpp
    $(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -c TestMRE.cpp -o TestMRE.o

Here, MRE.hpp and MRE.tpp are listed as dependencies,
so Make will recompile TestMRE.o when either file changes.
However, they do not appear in the compilation command,
because template implementation files (.tpp) are included by the .cpp through the .hpp

Using $^ in the link command would incorrectly pass MRE.tpp to the compiler, so the link rule must explicitly list only the object files.

Now, modifying MRE.tpp correctly triggers recompilation, and the program outputs:
final message

Q: Split Entry into Multiple Rows Based on Cell Value A:

if you set up a lookup table like this:

you can do just:

=REDUCE(TOCOL(,1), TOCOL(H2:H, 1), LAMBDA(i, h, IFERROR(VSTACK(i, 
 LET(r, FILTER(A:F, C:C=h), QUERY(REDUCE(r, 
 SEQUENCE(COLUMNS(IFERROR(SPLIT(VLOOKUP(h, H:I, 2), ","), 1))), 
 LAMBDA(x, y, IFERROR(VSTACK(x, HSTACK(CHOOSECOLS(r, 1,2), 
 INDEX(TOCOL(SPLIT(VLOOKUP(INDEX(r,,3), H:I, 2), ",")), y), INDEX(r,,4), 
 INDEX(r,,5)/COLUMNS(IFERROR(SPLIT(VLOOKUP(INDEX(r,,3), H:I, 2), ","), 1)),
 INDEX(r,,6)))))), "offset 1", ))))))

or this to include non-groups:

=VSTACK(FILTER(A2:F, C2:C<>"", NOT(REGEXMATCH(C2:C, "Group"))), 
 REDUCE(TOCOL(,1), TOCOL(H2:H, 1), LAMBDA(i, h, IFERROR(VSTACK(i, 
 LET(r, FILTER(A:F, C:C=h), QUERY(REDUCE(r, 
 SEQUENCE(COLUMNS(IFERROR(SPLIT(VLOOKUP(h, H:I, 2), ","), 1))), 
 LAMBDA(x, y, IFERROR(VSTACK(x, HSTACK(CHOOSECOLS(r, 1,2), 
 INDEX(TOCOL(SPLIT(VLOOKUP(INDEX(r,,3), H:I, 2), ",")), y), INDEX(r,,4), 
 INDEX(r,,5)/COLUMNS(IFERROR(SPLIT(VLOOKUP(INDEX(r,,3), H:I, 2), ","), 1)),
 INDEX(r,,6)))))), "offset 1", )))))))

and from there a simple sum if needed:

=QUERY(VSTACK(FILTER(A2:F, C2:C<>"", NOT(REGEXMATCH(C2:C, "Group"))), 
 REDUCE(TOCOL(,1), TOCOL(H2:H, 1), LAMBDA(i, h, IFERROR(VSTACK(i, 
 LET(r, FILTER(A:F, C:C=h), QUERY(REDUCE(r, 
 SEQUENCE(COLUMNS(IFERROR(SPLIT(VLOOKUP(h, H:I, 2), ","), 1))), 
 LAMBDA(x, y, IFERROR(VSTACK(x, HSTACK(CHOOSECOLS(r, 1,2), 
 INDEX(TOCOL(SPLIT(VLOOKUP(INDEX(r,,3), H:I, 2), ",")), y), INDEX(r,,4), 
 INDEX(r,,5)/COLUMNS(IFERROR(SPLIT(VLOOKUP(INDEX(r,,3), H:I, 2), ","), 1)),
 INDEX(r,,6)))))), "offset 1", ))))))), 
 "select Col1,Col2,Col3,Col4,sum(Col5),Col6 
  group by Col1,Col2,Col3,Col4,Col6 label sum(Col5)''")
